content: The 2018 baseline survey titled Needs to Support On-Farm Biodiversity for Healthy People in Resilient Landscapes highlights the importance of promoting agricultural biodiversity to enhance human health and environmental resilience. A related publication by Boedecker et al. (2019) demonstrated that participatory farm diversification and nutrition education significantly improved dietary diversity in Western Kenya, as published in Maternal & Child Nutrition. The ENRICH Project in Kenya, reported by Nutrition International in 2019, conducted formative research to address nutritional gaps. Similarly, Robert et al. (2021) utilized formative research to design interventions involving animal-source foods and micronutrient powders to improve nutrient intake among infants and young children in Tanzania, Kenya, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, as published in Maternal & Child Nutrition. In Malawi, data from the iLiNS-DOSE trial, provided by Hemsworth, Ferguson, and Tampere University, revealed that lipid-based nutrient supplements increased energy and macronutrient intake among infants, as published in The Journal of Nutrition (2016). Another study from the Malawi Mazira trial, shared by Caswell and Arnold, showed that egg-based complementary feeding improved energy intake and dietary diversity, as reported in Maternal & Child Nutrition (2021). In Nigeria, De Moura et al. (2015) examined cassava intake and its impact on vitamin A status among women and preschool children in Akwa-Ibom, published in PLOS One. In Senegal, the ARCH Project analyzed child feeding practices, with Pries et al. (2017) reporting high consumption of commercially produced snack foods and sugar-sweetened beverages during complementary feeding periods in urban African and Asian contexts, as published in Maternal & Child Nutrition. In South Africa, Faber (2005) highlighted the inadequacy of micronutrient content in complementary foods consumed by rural infants aged 6–12 months, as published in Public Health Nutrition. In Tanzania, the ENRICH Project conducted formative research to address nutritional challenges, as reported by Nutrition International in 2019. In Zambia, data from the 2009 Food Consumption and Vitamin A Status Survey, provided by the Tropical Diseases Research Centre and other organizations, focused on vitamin A and maize intake among women and children. Hotz et al. (2012) linked vitamin A intake and infections to plasma retinol levels in preschool children, as published in Public Health Nutrition. In Brazil, data from the 2019 National Survey on Child Nutrition (ENANI) were analyzed to assess dietary patterns, with Alves-Santos et al. (2021) detailing methodological aspects in Cadernos de Saúde Pública. The PROPAN study in Brazil, Jamaica, Mexico, and Panama, led by Frongillo et al. (2003), aimed to prevent early childhood malnutrition by improving complementary feeding practices. In Colombia, Tharrey et al. (2017) adapted new food-based complementary feeding recommendations using linear programming, as published in Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition. In Ecuador, data from the 2011–2013 ENSANUT survey were harmonized for global dietary databases. In Guatemala, the Optifood study identified nutritional gaps among children and mothers, as reported by INCAP and partners in 2016. In Mexico, the 2012 National Health and Nutrition Survey provided insights into dietary practices, harmonized for global databases. In Peru, data from a 2015 baseline survey in Huancavelica assessed dietary intake among infants and young children before an intervention promoting Andean agrobiodiversity. This project was led by Grupo Yanapai and the Instituto de Investigación Nutricional. In Bangladesh, the ENRICH Project conducted formative research to improve nutrition, as reported by Nutrition International in 2019. In Cambodia, the ARCH Project analyzed child feeding practices, with Pries et al. providing tabulated data. In China, Wu et al. (2013) used a multi-method approach to improve nutritious food intake among children aged 6–23 months in Wuyi County, as published in Croatian Medical Journal. In India, data from the National Institute of Nutrition highlighted dietary and nutritional status among rural populations. In Indonesia, the ARCH Project revealed high consumption of commercially produced snack foods among children under three in Bandung City, as reported by Green et al. (2019) in Maternal & Child Nutrition. The SMILING Project also explored food-based approaches to improve dietary adequacy in Southeast Asia. In Israel, the MABAT Infant National Health and Nutrition Survey (2009–2012) provided insights into infant feeding practices. In Korea, the 2017 KNHANES survey contributed to global dietary databases. In Laos, the SMILING Project assessed food-based strategies for women and children. In Nepal, the ARCH Project linked unhealthy snack consumption to lower dietary adequacy and growth outcomes among young children, as reported by Pries et al. (2019) in The Journal of Nutrition. In Pakistan, the ENRICH Project conducted formative research to address nutritional challenges, while the Optifood study analyzed dietary costs and adequacy across districts. In Singapore, Lim et al. (2018) examined food sources of energy and macronutrients among infants aged 6–12 months, as published in International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. In Thailand, the SMILING Project evaluated food-based strategies for dietary adequacy. In Vietnam, the SMILING Project assessed food-based approaches for women and children. In Europe, the EU Childhood Obesity Project (CHOP) linked early dietary patterns to mid-childhood outcomes, as reported by Luque et al. (2018) in The Journal of Nutrition. In Bulgaria, the NUTRICHILD study assessed nutritional status among children under five. In the Czech Republic, Kudlova and Rames (2007) analyzed food consumption patterns among infants and toddlers in Prague. In France, Yuan et al. In Germany, the DONALD Study provided longitudinal dietary data. In Portugal, the IAN-AF survey (2015–2016) contributed to European and global dietary databases. In the UK, the 2011 Diet and Nutrition Survey of Infants and Young Children provided nationally representative data. In Australia, Mauch et al. (2017) analyzed food consumption patterns among toddlers, while Byrne et al. (2016) examined maternal perceptions of toddler weight status. In New Zealand, Szmyd-Gay et al. (2010) quantified food consumption among toddlers.
